\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\usepackage{booktabs}
\usepackage{amsmath}

\title{Canopy and Ripening Management in a Cool-Climate Vineyard}
\author{L. Marchetti and P. Aalto}
\date{July 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\section{Site and Planting Material}
The vineyard sits on a southeast-facing slope at 340~m elevation,
with gravelly limestone soils over a fractured marl bedrock.
Rows run north--south at 2.4~m spacing with 1.0~m between vines,
giving 4167 vines per hectare across the seven blocks.
The scion is Vitis_vinifera cv. Pinot Noir grafted onto 41B rootstock,
chosen for its tolerance of active lime and its moderate vigour.
Clones 115 and 667 occupy alternating panels of six rows each.
Drainage tiles were renewed in block #7 after the wet spring of 2024,
and that block now dries two days earlier than its neighbours.
\item Bird netting is deployed from the first sign of veraison.
The oldest plantings date from 1998 and are own-rooted replacements
of an earlier phylloxera-damaged parcel.

\section{Seasonal Heat Accumulation}
Growing degree days were tallied from budburst to harvest using
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{GDD} = \sum_{d=1}^{n} \max\!\left(0,\; \frac{T_{\max} + T_{\min}}{2} - 10\right),
\end{equation}
where daily temperatures come from the estate weather station
at the top of the slope.
The 2025 season accumulated 1187 degree days,
placing it between the warm 2022 and the cool 2021 vintages.
Budburst was recorded on 18~April,
flowering on 12~June,
and veraison began on 9~August in the earliest panels.
Rainfall to the end of August totalled 310~mm,
two thirds of it falling before flowering,
so the ripening months were dry and cool at night.
A light frost on 23~April singed the lowest rows of the valley block
but caused no measurable crop loss.
The station at the slope top ran without gaps all season,
and its logger was checked against a handheld sensor monthly.

\section{Canopy Management}
Canopy work followed the estate protocol through the season:
\begin{itemize}
\item Shoot thinning at 15~cm growth to eight shoots per metre of row.
\item Leaf removal on the morning side at fruit set,
repeated lightly where the canopy closed again.
\item Hedging twice, at veraison and three weeks later,
keeping the fruiting wall below the top wire.

\section{Irrigation and Floor Management}
No irrigation was needed until mid-July,
when the two youngest blocks received a single 12~mm pass
to carry them through the only real dry spell.
The permanent sward between the rows was mown three times
and left as mulch on the surface.
Alternate rows were cultivated shallowly in May
to keep the sward from competing during shoot growth.
By harvest the floor was firm enough for the picker trailer
on all but the two lowest rows.

\section{Pest and Disease Calendar}
Downy mildew pressure was moderate after the June rains;
sulphur and copper were applied on a ten-day schedule until bunch closure.
Powdery mildew appeared late on the shaded side of the lower blocks
and was held with two targeted sulphur passes.
No botrytis sprays were needed before harvest,
thanks to the open canopy and the dry September.

\section{Fruit Composition at Harvest}
Berry samples were taken weekly from veraison onward,
fifty berries per panel drawn from both sides of the row.
Juice was analysed for soluble solids, pH and titratable acidity.
Panel means at harvest are summarised below.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
Panel & Brix & pH & TA (g/L) \\
\midrule
115 north & 23.1 & 3.34 & 7.8 & \\
115 south & 23.6 & 3.31 & 7.5 \\
667 north & 22.8 & 3.29 & 8.1 \\
667 south & 23.4 & 3.36 & 7.6 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Harvest composition by clone and exposure\footnote{TA as tartaric acid equivalents.}}
\end{table}

The south-facing panels ran about half a degree Brix ahead
of the north-facing ones at every sampling date.
Titratable acidity stayed comfortably high in all panels,
as expected for the site and the season.

\section{Winemaking Notes}
Fruit was picked by hand in the morning and sorted at the winery.
Fermentation used ambient yeast in open vats
with twice-daily punchdowns over twelve days.
One third of the fruit went in as whole clusters
to lift the aromatic profile of the final blend.
Pressing was gentle, with the press fraction kept separate
and tasted before any blending decision.
The wine went to neutral oak for the winter
and will be racked once in the spring.
Malolactic fermentation finished in the barrel cellar
by the end of November without inoculation.
Sulphur additions were kept to a single post-malolactic dose,
adjusted against the measured free level each month.

\section{Discussion}
The season rewarded restraint in the canopy:
panels hedged hardest at fruit set ripened no faster
than those hedged lightly twice.
The morning-side leaf removal kept the afternoon fruit zone shaded,
which we credit for the retained acidity in a warm year.
Clone 667 again gave the deeper colour and the firmer acid line,
while clone 115 carried the aromatic detail.
The lower blocks remain the frost-prone spots,
and the fan budget for next spring has been increased accordingly.

Block by block, the ripening curves tracked the heat accumulation
with the usual lag after veraison.
Juice yields averaged 640 litres per tonne across the press fractions,
in line with the five-year estate mean.
The sorting table rejected very little fruit this season,
a sign that the disease calendar was well timed.
We will repeat the light-touch canopy regime next year
and extend the morning-side leaf removal to the nursery rows.
The tasting panel scored the 667 lots higher for structure
and the 115 lots higher for aroma,
so the blend will keep the two clones in their current shares.
Bottling is planned for the second week of September,
after a light polish filtration at the estate.

\section{Conclusion}
Moderate crop loads and an open canopy delivered clean, ripe fruit
despite the humid spells in early August.
The interplay of the two clones again proved valuable at blending,
and the heat-sum model tracked the observed ripening dates well.
The remaining weak points are the frost-prone lower rows
and the slow drainage after cloudbursts in the valley block;
both are scheduled for capital work over the winter.
The protocol is now stable enough to hand to the new vineyard manager
with only seasonal adjustments,
and the season's records have been archived with the estate ledgers.
\end{document}
